name: Triethanolamine (TEOA) was used as a sacrificial electron donor, reductant, or hole scavenger in photocatalytic and related photoinduced systems.
TEOA can reductively quench excited photosensitizers or oxidized intermediates, generating reduced species and supporting photoredox catalytic cycles.
Using TEOA can improve, alter, or sometimes worsen photocatalytic yield, selectivity, or rate depending on the system and concentration.
TEOA can act as a proton donor/source or as a base/proton acceptor in different mechanisms, and protonation can change its reduction behavior.
Many cited photocatalytic systems show little or no activity without TEOA; omitting it can stop product formation or make hole consumption rate-limiting.
TEOA can be oxidized or decomposed during photocatalysis to products such as glycolaldehyde, aldehydes, and diethanolamine, and these transformations can affect performance or deactivation.
TEOA and related sacrificial agents are criticized for drawbacks such as toxicity, cost, non-renewability, decomposition, low atom economy, and unsustainability.
TEOA can coordinate to metal centers or form CO2–TEOA and metal–TEOA adducts, influencing CO2 capture, redox equilibria, spectral behavior, intermediate stability, and catalyst durability.

TEOA is oxidized by photogenerated holes and participates in reductive-quenching/electron-transfer steps that complete the photocatalytic cycle, with reported radical formation, EPR changes, and oxidation products.
TEOA can be a poorer or detrimental donor/additive than alternatives and can lead to lower efficiency, deactivation, or unfavorable intermediate accumulation.
TEOA is discussed as a buffer or additive, and its molecular and redox/photophysical properties affect compatibility in photocatalytic setups.
TEOA can stabilize photocatalysts or suspensions through adsorption, hydrogen bonding, surface protection, or improved charge separation.

TEOA can participate in CO2 activation and proton-transfer chemistry, including stabilizing intermediates, supporting CO2–TEOA adducts, protonating bound CO2 or metalocarboxylates, and helping retain or activate CO2 in solution.
In some cited systems, TEOA did not quench the probed excited state or emission signal, or quenching was negligible.

TEOA is a commonly studied hole scavenger/electron donor, and high-concentration TEOA in DMF or DMA can enhance the durability, efficiency, and selectivity of photocatalytic CO2 reduction to CO compared with other solvents and additives.

In some CO2-reduction/photophysical contexts, TEOA was energetically or photophysically limiting rather than beneficial: its redox level was close to or below the catalysts' HOMO levels, it could not quench [Ru-bpy], CO2-reduction activity was much lower than H2 evolution despite TEOA, and TEOA could not reduce CO2 under photocatalytic conditions.
Relative to other donors or bases, TEOA can be better or worse for photocatalytic performance depending on the system and donor pair used.
TEOA was implicated in electron-transfer and radical pathways.
Changing TEOA concentration or excess can alter rate, intermediate buildup, conversion, and selectivity, and very high concentrations can be unfavorable.
Some claims explicitly qualify TEOA's mechanistic role or exclude simple causal interpretations, such as uncoupled photooxidation/NAD+ reduction, no reduction of 3ROH*, or unwanted side reactions.
Controls and interpretation of TEOA's own catalytic contribution must be considered in photocatalytic CO2-reduction studies, because secondary roles of TEOA can otherwise be overlooked.
Slow charge recombination and high oxidative power favor efficient TEOA oxidation and can reduce side reactions or decomposition in dyad systems.
As a base, TEOA can suppress charge recombination or back-electron transfer and alter protonation, hydride, and dimer kinetics, although these effects may be incomplete.

TEOA is an effective sacrificial electron donor that creates strongly reducing conditions, boosts H2 and formic acid formation, captures photogenerated holes to aid charge separation, and its consumption can lower C1 production rates
In irradiated TEOA aqueous systems, CO generation increases with irradiation time, requires UV light to initiate, and is accompanied by a new UV-vis band suggesting a carbamate intermediate.

When TEOA is present as a sacrificial donor, catalyst activity and CO attribution must be interpreted carefully because TEOA contributes to the observed process; CO production can drop in H2O/TEOA and controls show CO is not necessarily from TEOA or polymeric carbon nitride decomposition

TEOA was less effective than ascorbic acid and more effective than cysteine for photocatalytic NADH regeneration; EDTA had a similar redox potential, and the yield differences may be explained by different oxidation mechanisms and reaction kinetics.
TEOA is the abbreviation for triethanolamine.
